passage: Sabina, I'll tell you about the winter I turned twenty-five, when my friend Anil died. He was twenty-six. I, Karthik, didn't believe it until I stood at the rites, and even then my hands felt like someone else's. For a week I buried myself in work and told everyone I was fine. It didn't hold. One night I heard his laugh in an old voice note and finally cried on the office stairs. After that I did things properly. I went to his family's house and sat with his mother, and we swapped stories about him until we were both laughing and crying. I checked on them every month. Some days I still feel unsafe, but the grief stopped being a wall and became a room I can enter.

qa.q: How old was Anil when he died?
Why did Karthik keep telling everyone "I'm fine" while burying himself in work?
qa.a: Karthik was avoiding the grief and trying to numb it, but it did not hold, and it broke through at the sound of Anil's laugh in the voice note.

qa.q: What did Karthik do that helped both Karthik and Anil's family?
qa.a: Karthik attended the rites, cried, swapped stories with Anil's mother and checked on the family every month.

qa.q: How might Anil's mother have felt when Karthik visited and shared stories?
qa.a: Probably comforted, not alone in remembering her son, laughing and crying together. 🤍

grounding: A friend dies young; grief is allowed to be messy, with rites, stories, tears and checking on the family instead of numbing with work.
